editorial.summary: Part Two resumes without a new introduction and first tests whether David Choe's phone relationship is meaningful despite never meeting. An unrelated story about a formerly known woman now reportedly homeless, using meth and being raped by a group is preserved as a secondhand allegation while protecting the vulnerable private person. The caller receives the alias Angel. David's therapist reportedly says he has never seemed happier; Asa asks whether distance permits feeling without ordinary relationship responsibility. David declares monogamy after one week and tells prior partners the sexual relationships are over. Bill Poon arrives dressed for a funeral on the wrong date, letting the room recap the story and revisit whether DVDASA helps anyone. Listener messages describe companionship during rehab or suicidal periods, but the cast weighs that against entertainment, exposure and the availability of real therapy. David describes crying, renewed concern for other people and buying unproven 'post-stroke' supplements for Angel's father. He and friends perform increasingly invasive identity checks. A Hawaii friend finally reverse-searches Angel's photos and identifies them as images of public model Jaclyn Swedberg. Angel later admits using another person's photos and says the deception went farther than intended. This establishes catfishing; it does not authenticate her name, alleged real photo, salon, ethnicity, family, father, stroke, charities, stalkers, cancer connections or social graph. David initially imagines violent retaliation, then calls his therapist and de-escalates. He knowingly keeps the fantasy going for one final day, falsely implies he knew all along, and sends novelty genital and body images as his own counter-deception. He admits beauty was central to his attraction, contradicting earlier claims that sex, body or gender would not matter. The trust breach, not the caller's ordinary appearance, becomes the reason he says a relationship is impossible. Crucially, he also acknowledges that she tried to stop on the first day and that he refused to let the contact end; the Part One panic and parking-lot vigil remain coercive pressure rather than retroactive romance. The cast debates cancer fraud, small-island exposure, fantasy, AI intimacy, chat-room deception, body dysmorphia, race and readiness for love. David considers meeting Angel or bringing her onto the show, but neither happens in this source. He offers to fund Valentin's education and returns to whether art can be created from peace rather than anger. Every idea, slur, contradiction and allegation remains attributable. Private identity trails and intimate images do not. Two empty zero-duration records are the only cleaner drops, and no named dialogue is published.
